https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/07/28/r.text: ILOILO CITY — Three seafarers from Iloilo are seeking immediate repatriation after surviving a drone attack on their cargo vessel in Ukraine, with their families appealing to the government to bring them home amid fears for their safety.Cynthia Dario, head of the Iloilo provincial Public Employment Service Office, said the families of the distressed seafarers sought PESO’s assistance on Monday to facilitate the seafarers’ return to the Philippines.The three Ilonggo crew members are among the 22 Filipino seafarers aboard MV Inase, which was struck by a military drone while docked at the Port of Pivdennyi in Ukraine on July 18.The Ilonggo seafarers are from Barangay Ilajas in Dingle, Barangay Mat-y in Miag-ao, and Barangay Ortiz in Iloilo City’s City Proper district.According to reports, a drone missile hit the sea vessel’s B Deck superstructure while it was docked at the port, sparking a fire and causing extensive damage to the accommodation area.Two crew members reportedly sustained injuries — an able seaman who suffered a head injury and a second officer who injured his hand.“The families came to our office because they want their relatives to be repatriated. They are now in Romania, but the seafarers fear they are still not safe because of their situation,” Dario said.She said the provincial government is expediting efforts to bring the seafarers home.“We are fast-tracking the repatriation. We are coordinating with the Department of Migrant Workers and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration to help bring them back to the Philippines as soon as possible,” she said.Following the attack, MV Inase sailed to Constanța, Romania, for inspection, but the crew members remained aboard the vessel.In a Facebook post on Sunday, the seafarer from Miagao, Ram-Ram Cerbo, appealed for immediate disembarkation, saying the crew continues to suffer from severe trauma following the attack.“Thank you, Lord, for the second life. We survived, although I sustained minor injuries. The important thing is that we are alive,” he wrote.The seafarer claimed that despite the incident, the vessel’s principal, Evalend Shipping Co., has yet to allow the affected Filipino crew members to disembark.He said they were instead instructed to remain on board and proceed to Turkey, a voyage that would require crossing the Black Sea.The Russia-Ukraine war has turned parts of the Black Sea into an active conflict zone, where merchant ships face risk of missile, drone, mine and port-strike attacks.“We have the right to disembark because of the severe trauma caused by the drone attack that happened during our transit in Odesa, Ukraine, on July 18. It has already been one week, and we still have not been allowed to go home. We are appealing to anyone who can help us,” the seafarer wrote.

http://www.theuknews.com/news/279222963/.text: AI before AI: The legacy of Norbert Wieners cybernetics (3/3) France24 05 Aug 2026, 11:05 GMT+10 The story of the founding fathers ofartificial intelligencealmost always features British mathematicianAlan Turingand his computing machine. John von Neumann is often presented as the mastermind behind programmable computers. Names from theDartmouth groupsuch as John McCarthy or Marvin Minsky are also sometimes cited as the inventors of artificial intelligence. However, another figure is often overlooked or relegated to the category of second-rate pioneers: Norbert Wiener, the founding father of cybernetics in the 1940s. ChatGPT,Claudeand the like can be regarded as the offspring of his ideas. But whether Wiener, with his moral, political and scientific convictions, would acknowledge the authorship of these modern large language models is uncertain. A young prodigy Wiener was born on November 26, 1894, in Columbia, Missouri, into a family of Jewish immigrants from EasternEurope. His father, Leo Wiener a highly strict professor of Slavic languages of Lithuanian origin would behave somewhat like Pygmalion and attempt to mould his son in his own image", said Pierre Cassou-Nogus, a philosopher atParis8 University and author of afictionalised account of the mathematicians life. "At least, that is how Wiener describes it in his autobiography, he added. Thus, Wiener became a young scientific prodigy moulded by his father, said Mathieu Triclot, a philosopher specialising in thehistoryof technology at the Belfort-Montbliard University of Technology. He learnt to read before the age of four, graduated from high school at 11, earned a bachelors degree in mathematics at 14 and completed his PhD in mathematics at Harvard at 18. A few years later, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) appointed him as one of its youngest professors. It was in this role that, afterWorld War II, Wiener developed his ideas which would have an impact on many fields related to artificial intelligence such as robotics, control engineering and multi-agent systems, said Philippe Mathieu, an artificial intelligence specialist at the University ofLille. Read moreAI before AI: The forgotten Soviet programme (1/2) Thesciencebehind cybernetics laid the foundations as early as 1943 in aseminal articleand is described in detail in the book Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, published in 1948. Cybernetics studies certain phenomena of control and information transmission in the same way in humans, in the animal kingdom and in the world of machines, Cassou-Nogus said. In other words, for Wiener and cyberneticists, it is possible to draw parallels between the way the human brain and a machine process the information they receive. Cybernetics, a super-science attracting the biggest names in AI In practical terms, these principles inspired Wiener to work on a new kind of anti-aircraft defence system during World War II. He aimed to create a system capable of adapting in real time to the movements of missiles or aircraft and of learning from its mistakes. These were the very first tentative steps towards what we would now call machine learning. The central theme of cybernetics is understanding how an entity adapts to its environment and to the information available. Intelligence is seen as the result of interactions between an entity [living or not] and its environment, Mathieu said. Logic, mathematics and electrical engineering, information theory, brain research and psychology a whole bundle of scientific disciplines influenced the events that led to AI,"writes Rudolf Seising, who specialises in the history ofscienceand technology at the Deutsches Museum in Munich. "In the first half of the 20th century, interdisciplinary considerations and, above all, transdisciplinary approaches to AI were mainly found under the umbrella of cybernetics, a super science. This jack-of-all-trades aspect of cybernetics may also explain why Wiener is less often seen as the father of AI than Turing or von Neumann, who had a more direct and immediate impact on the development of computer science. Read moreThe Dartmouth Workshop: The $7,500 investment that gave birth to AI (2/2) But for Triclot, cybernetics indirect influence on AI is considerable. A series of ten meetings the Macy Conferences on Cybernetics brought together scientists interested in Wieners ideas between 1946 and 1953. Some of the biggest names in the history of AI, such as von Neumann and Claude Shannon, took part and identified themselves with cybernetics at the time. One of the founding members of the Macy Conferences was the psychologist Joseph Carl Robnett Licklider, one of the central figures in the history of American computing, said Triclot. He later became the head of the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. He then "played a key role in the funding and development of the internet and also took an interest in human-computer interface technologies in the 1960s, added Triclot. At MIT, Wiener also supervised the work of another researcher who was pivotal to the development of modern AI: Walter Pitts. In the 1940s, this logician laid the foundations for the first neural network model. The Manhattan Project This work, which is rooted in cybernetics, is essential to understanding todays large language models. Whilst cybernetics itself may now seem a relic of the past, it paved the way, alongside neural networks, for the emergence of the branch of AI known as connectionism, which lies at the heart of the rise of ChatGPT and other 21st-century AI systems. Wiener not only provided an intellectual cradle for AI, but he was also one of the first to warn of its dangers, Cassou-Nogus said. Known for his strong-willed character and notorious outbursts of anger, Wiener understood why certain areas of scientific research were dangerous.Consequently, he refused to take part in the Manhattan Project, which led to the development of the first atomic bomb. Following the bombings ofHiroshimaandNagasaki, Wiener even published a famousopen letterin which he stated his intention to no longer publish research that could be misused for creating weapons of mass destruction. Albert Einstein supported the move at the time. But with cybernetics, he also foresaw as early as 1948, the possibility of a fully or almost fully automated society. A development which, in his view, could just as easily lead humanity to a world free from the constraints of work or to a social hell of mass unemployment, Cassou-Nogus said. Wiener concluded that he should not abandon his work, precisely so that he could influence the direction of research in his field. Often labelled as politically left-wing US authorities suspected that he was sympathetic to the Soviet bloc during theCold WarWiener was thus one of the first to warn of the risk of social upheaval linked to the advent of machines. In this sense, cybernetics is a profoundly political endeavour, also driven by this fear of technological unemployment caused by machines that could replace workers, said Triclot. For him, it is striking to read this as early as 1947, at a time when computers were still very rare. But for Wiener, this risk would only materialise if we fall into the trap of treating human beings inhumanely, said Triclot. In other words, according to Wiener, robots would only be able to replace humans if we reduced humans to the status of robots by denying everything that distinguishes human beings from machines. Even though the term cybernetics seems to have fallen out of use, the ideas of its founder are relevant today, at a time when companies are citing the triumph of AI to justify masslayoffs. https://www.express.co.uk/news/world/223.text: Home News World The discovery comes amid concerns that the nation is weaponising migration against the EU (Image: Getty) Authorities in a northern EU nation have discovered a tunnel used by migrants to cross its border from Belarus illegally for the first time. On Monday (August 10), border guards in Latvia caught 15 people who had travelled through a 33-foot-long (10m) tunnel near the border fence from the Eastern European country, Riga’s Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said on Tuesday. It comes amid growing concerns that Minsk is weaponising migration against the bloc. Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko is a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his regime has supported Moscow’s war against Ukraine and taken a hostile stance toward the EU . Tunnels have previously been found in Lithuania, according to Baltic media, but this is the first time one has been used to cross into Latvia. "No signs of violations had previously been detected in this exact location, and no detentions of persons illegally crossing the state border had occurred there." Authorities returned all 15 people to their “country of departure” and are continuing to inspect the area around the tunnel. Latvia has since launched an operation to strengthen its border security, known as Operation "Werewolf" (Vilkatis), announced by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs. The operation – which integrates the military, police and border guards under unified crisis management – is scheduled to run until the end of August. https://www.politico.eu/article/brussels.text: Police and military patrols arrested a man at Brussels’ Gare du Midi after customs officers found a Kalashnikov rifle in his bag during a security check, according to Belgian media . Interior Minister Bernard Quintin seized on the arrest to defend the government’s decision to deploy joint security patrols at Brussels train and metro stations. “Thank you to the services for their swift and decisive action,” Quintin wrote on X. “This demonstrates that strengthening patrols in train stations and subways with the help of our military is crucial and must be continued, or even expanded.” Advertisement Advertisement The suspect had recently arrived by train from France. He was not brandishing the rifle inside the station, according to reports. Investigators are still working to establish why he was carrying the weapon. Gare du Midi, Belgium’s main international rail gateway, has long struggled with crime and insecurity. Around 3,500 offenses were recorded there annually between 2018 and 2022 — roughly as many as across stations in 13 major Flemish cities combined. Theft, extortion and drug-related offenses were among the most common. The arrest comes after another burst of gun violence around southern Brussels. Several shootings hit nearby Saint-Gilles in late August, leaving people injured, while police detained suspects and seized military-grade firearms.

Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters UK security and counter-terrorism Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Mon 12 Oct 2026 13.08 EDT First published on Mon 12 Oct 2026 11.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month. The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC in the aftermath of an ambiguous episode that, despite over a fortnight of police investigation, has yet to lead to anybody being charged. After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran? Read more Addressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran , almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.” 22:58 Was Burnham right to talk about Russian interference in Brexit? | Politics Weekly In a statement to the House of Commons, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, told MPs that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had summoned the Iranian ambassador over the Fairford incident and that the government had imposed sanctions on two individuals accused of spying in Europe and the US. “He [Miliband] will condemn Iran’s continued attempts to undermine our safety. We are also sanctioning two individuals involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of the government of Iran in Europe and the US, and we will not hesitate to take further action to restrict Iran’s capacity to threaten international security,” she said. Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found. However, the incident was followed by the withdrawal of 12 B-1 bombers a week later, amid reports that the US was concerned about a possible drone attack on a base it had used to attack Iran during the Middle East war in the spring and summer. Burnham’s brief remarks were a step up from previous comments. The prime minister had said in the days after the incident that there were “strong indications” Iran had played a part – but now appeared confident enough to apportion responsibility. A joint statement from the UK, US and other European allies, released by the Foreign Office, added that the UK “has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors”. ​However, despite his statement, it remains unclear what the authorities think happened at Fairford. Some experts have speculated it was a “feint” to demonstrate that Iran could in theory attack a relatively open site. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion British sources have repeatedly maintained that Iran lacks the capability to launch what would be a sophisticated drone attack, but the incident appears to have unnerved the US, which is worried about the security of its bases in Europe. The incident at Fairford comes after what the UK, in the joint statement, said was a recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and US interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI). Though the US has detained and indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, whom it accuses of being behind the HAYI group, there is evidence to suggest that Iran-linked attacks have continued. A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb. Prosecutors told a magistrates court the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The Big Build royal commission has heard evidence about the growing influence of CFMEU in Victoria. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP View image in fullscreen The Big Build royal commission has heard evidence about the growing influence of CFMEU in Victoria. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Victorian politics CFMEU ‘enjoy a significant level of influence’ over Victorian government, Big Build royal commission hears Inquiry into allegations of corruption begins block of hearings focused on 2022 level crossing removal project Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Nino Bucci and Jack Larkin Sun 8 Nov 2026 23.34 EST Last modified on Mon 9 Nov 2026 03.44 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian Big Build projects has heard a major construction company feared putting the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) offside because of its close links to the Daniel Andrews Labor government. The first block of hearings under the commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria will hear evidence about the union’s involvement in a level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north of Melbourne, in 2022. The project involved the removal of a level crossing and the construction of a new rail bridge and underpass. A Big Build royal commission helped Ben Carroll become premier. Will it be his downfall? Read more The counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, said 20 witnesses have been compelled to appear during the November hearings. But he warned that others were not complying with orders to produce documents to the commission, including using the excuse of “government policy” to delay their production. Failing to comply with such orders is a criminal offence. “It is extremely concerning that some parties have not complied with the terms of those notices to produce,” Young said. The hearings in November will focus on what government officials did during a June 2022 meeting in order to appease the union, who had forced work to stop on the Gap Road project. Young showed the commission evidence that – in the years before the union interfered in the project – there was increasing awareness within the construction sector about the prospect of industrial action curtailing work, and the growing influence of the CFMEU. He said that in 2017, one of the companies involved in the Gap Road project, John Holland, noted that the CFMEU was “proud of the fact that none of their site visits are code compliant”. It also noted in an email the “significance of the CFMEU relationship with the Andrews government in Victoria, and the impact this is having, and will have in the future, in respect of client relationships with the Victorian government”. Such was the extent of that relationship that John Holland officials suspected the CFMEU would have a “substantial amount of knowledge around proposed government tenders and input” in respect of the tender process. “We are thus particularly mindful of the optics in our interactions with union stakeholders,” the 2017 email said. Four years later, the construction company noted that “the CFMEU are emboldened by their success on major infrastructure projects,” and later in 2021, that they “enjoy a significant level of influence within the state government”. “It is a level of influence not seen in previous years and is unlikely to diminish.” Police called to dispute Young told the hearing that four of the CFMEU officials who would later force work to stop at Gap Road had similarly interfered in the Metro Tunnel project . He said the officials entered the Gap Road project’s eastern portal 29 times in January 2020, and were involved in activity considered to be unlawful, but nonetheless received attention from the government, which asked if the safety issues they raised were valid. Young said that a “very high risk rating” was applied to the possibility of industrial action on Gap Road. But he said that it was not until May 2022 where this risk escalated, and CFMEU officials more regularly appeared on site. By early June, the health and safety manager for the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project, Neil Thompson, was calling police, desperate for their help in removing union officials who were stopping work including by sitting on barriers and refusing to move. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Young tendered internal notes taken on the union activity that showed there were references to the CFMEU officials warning workers that “you guys better not turn up tonight otherwise we will smash you during the day,” and that “their life would be [made] very difficult for them personally” if they continued working on the project. A recording of a phone call between Thompson and WorkSafe and a subsequent email showed that on 6 June – the day before a meeting that is central to the commission’s hearings – he was unclear about how to get work to continue on site. Thompson stressed the need for the union to be removed, given trains had been stopped on the line in order for a bridge to be built. “We actually called Victoria police to escort themself off site,” Thompson said in the call to WorkSafe. “Victoria police said there was nothing they could do. We’re going around in circles a bit because last week WorkSafe said there was nothing they could do. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We’re just having to put up with no work happening at the moment.” The following day, Young said, there was a 13-minute meeting, followed by a subsequent meeting at the CFMEU, which resolved the issues. Two CFMEU officials, Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas, attended the meeting along with four officials from the project, Young told the hearing. Young said that while the commission had obtained significant documentation regarding the events leading up to the meeting, little was known about what occurred during it and why it was significant, so the commission would be reliant on the memory witnesses had of conversations four years ago. The key questions included what stopped the work, and whether those disruptions were used as leverage by the CFMEU, he said. It remained unclear exactly how much the CFMEU disruption to works on the site had cost, nor what the cost was to end the disruption, Young said. But the union interrupted work on the site for 36 hours – and traffic controllers employed after the disruption charged significantly more than those previously employed, documents in evidence before the commission show. The hourly rate increased from about $45 to $88, or from $59 to $147 for penalty rates, the documents show. This meant, for example, that one 10-and-a-half hour shift cost $609 under the previous firm, but $1225 for the same shift under the new firm, Young said. The Major Transport Infrastructure Authority director general started considering the cost implications of a CFMEU campaign to increase the rates of traffic controllers about the same time the disruptions occurred on the Gap Road project. A September briefing prepared for the then minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan, estimated that the changes could cost the authority $60m to $78m for current projects, and well in excess of $400m for those projects in planning.
